news.title: Taiwan 'Urgently Needs' $14 Billion US Arms, Says Deal 'Up To' Trump
news.text: The timing of Washington's $14 billion arms sales package to Taiwan is "very much up to" President Donald Trump and will not be affected by the US midterm results, according to a Taiwanese government official.Taiwan has been waiting months for Trump to approve the record sale of weapons and equipment that the island says it needs to strengthen its defence capabilities to deter a potential Chinese attack.Beijing claims the island democracy is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex it.Trump has stalled the arms sale, saying in May it could be used as a bargaining chip with China, as the two superpowers tried to ease trade tensions."When it comes to time, I think it's very much up to... President Trump," said Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi.Taiwan enjoys "very strong bipartisan support" from Congress, and this month's midterm results, which saw Democrats win control of the House and Senate, would not affect the timing, Chen said.READ | Taiwan Receives First US-Made F-16V Fighter Jets Amid China ThreatThe Trump administration had to consider "many factors" when it came to arms sales to Taiwan, including the Middle East war."We respect that, but at the same time, we express that we really have an urgent need for those capabilities," Chen said.Patriot missiles, an automated command and control system and a 360-degree air defence radar system are among the items in the $14 billion package.Chen said Taiwan had "very good direct communication" with the Trump administration and "we are reassured that that will not change"."This could be just a matter of time before" the sale is approved, either as one package or in smaller parcels, he said.Taiwan 'Structurally Important'Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third and fourth time this year at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen this week and at the G20 in the United States in December.While Taiwan has been on the agenda at previous talks between the rival leaders, Chen brushed off concerns about the upcoming meetings."We are very confident and very comfortable with our relationship with the US and with other like-minded partners," Chen said.READ | Trump Asked Xi In White House If China Wants To Buy American Weapons: Envoy"We are structurally important, and our people (are) committed to our own defence. I think this (is) what matters the most," he said."And Taiwan stands in the middle of the whole AI revolution. I think that now almost every leader in the world understands the situation."Taiwan is a powerhouse in the global semiconductor industry, producing nearly all of the most advanced chips for companies including Nvidia and Apple.After Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who US intelligence agencies believe is spying for Beijing, Chen said the case underlines the need to be "very vigilant about China".China is "very aggressive" when it comes to stealing intellectual property and technology to get around export controls, Chen said.Huang, who regularly visited Taiwan to see Nvidia's clients, including TSMC, and had been seen in the capital Taipei with the Chinese woman, would be welcome back to the island, said Chen."He certainly will be welcome but I think... every business leader in the world has to learn this lesson that China is trying to poach your trade secrets," he said."They are going to arrange (a) spy in your life so that they can get easier access."Beijing has rejected the allegations as "entirely baseless".China is in a race for tech dominance against the United States, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips.Taiwan has long accused China of carrying out espionage activities on the island, including targeting its tech sector.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Trump has stalled the arms sale, saying in May it could be used as a bargaining chip with China, as the two superpowers tried to ease trade tensions.
news.author: Agence France Presse

news.title: Asia data center hotbed hit by U.S. chip curbs as Trump visits
news.text: U.S. President Donald Trump is targeting Southeast Asia in Washington’s rush to tighten China’s access to the world’s most advanced chips, with his administration announcing new rules just before he travels to the region.Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers, according to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department.The region has seen a boom in data centers housing the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models. Some of that demand has come remotely from firms based in China including Alibaba Group Holding and Bytedance, whose access to the most-advanced chips Washington wants to block.
news.summary: Operators in Southeast Asia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers.
news.author: The Japan Times,Web Master

news.title: 'Bring Jensen Back': Nvidia dismisses campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate former CEO
news.text: Nvidia's board is reportedly not considering bringing back co-founder Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer (CEO), despite growing support from US President Donald Trump, Elon Musk and several prominent technology leaders for his reinstatement. According to a CNBC report cited by Hindustan Times, the company's board is currently focused on investigating allegations involving Huang and is not holding discussions about his possible return. An anonymous source familiar with the matter said the board was not considering reinstating the former CEO. An online petition demanding Huang's return has gathered around 180,000 signatures, with Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among those supporting the campaign. Donald Trump backs Jensen Huang's return US President Donald Trump has also voiced support for Huang's possible return to the chipmaker. Speaking to reporters on Monday while leaving the White House for a trip to the Philippines and China, Trump said he would not mind seeing the former Nvidia chief reinstated. "I would certainly not mind seeing that," Trump said, adding that Huang had learnt a big lesson and that many people wanted him back at the company. Trump's remarks have added to the growing campaign for Huang's reinstatement, even as Nvidia's board appears unwilling to reconsider its decision. Elon Musk and tech leaders support Huang Musk has publicly backed the campaign to bring Huang back to Nvidia, joining several prominent technology executives who believe the company should reconsider its leadership decision. The petition has attracted support from Silicon Valley leaders and thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees. Supporters have also questioned the circumstances surrounding Huang's departure and called for the company to give him a fair hearing. Meanwhile, investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management have urged Nvidia's board to carefully evaluate its next leadership moves, highlighting Huang's contribution to the company's growth and the unanswered questions surrounding his exit. Why did Jensen Huang step down as Nvidia CEO? Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO last week after leading the company he co-founded for 33 years. His departure followed his admission of an affair, while reports also raised questions about his relationships with employees and Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who was accused of having links to Chinese intelligence. The allegations prompted concerns about potential national security risks and whether confidential company information could have been exposed. Nvidia has appointed law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang's conduct. The company's board also appointed former acting US attorney Joon H. Kim to lead an independent investigation into the matter. Following Huang's resignation, Nvidia's board appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a successor. Despite the growing public support for Huang, the company's immediate focus remains on the investigation and its leadership transition.
news.summary: Huang stepped down following allegations involving personal relationships and concerns over possible Chinese intelligence links. Nvidia has appointed an independent investigator and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
news.author: Zayan Mirza

news.title: Trump in Philippines: Expected to meet regional partners, talk trade and seek respite from troubles at home
news.text: MANILA: President Donald Trump lands in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he's expected to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.It's his first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.When Trump arrives Tuesday in Manila, he'll get all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have particularly escalated in recent years between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.Shortly after Trump arrives in the Philippines, he heads to a meeting with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations including the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that has aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be the first meeting of the Quad leaders since Trump returned to the White House last year..Elon Musk expected to accompany Trump on China visit; Iran on agenda for trilateral talks with Xi, Putin.Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.The U.S. had announced a trade framework with Thailand last October in which that nation would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration had said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.Now 97 and wheelchair-bound, the former jetset Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president had partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a Philippine strongman, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press."Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said. "He has asked President Marcos in phone calls, 'I know your mother, how is she?'"When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit..Trump says he may meet Kim Jong Un in China, hints at discussing Nvidia with Xi.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Inside Deutsche Bank: Leak of 15 million files exposes secrets, scandals and double standards of global financial giant
news.text:
More than 15 million internal files. Emails from senior executives. Secret risk assessments. Suspicious transaction reports. Private information about billionaires, oligarchs, politicians and royalty. Records involving Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein and sanctioned businessmen. Previously undisclosed companies linked to authoritarian regimes.

Together, they add up to the largest cache of internal documents ever leaked to journalists from within a bank.

For months, more than 200 reporters from around the world examined the huge cache as part of an investigation called Inside Deutsche Bank. The records span some of the bank’s most sensitive functions and activities: anti-financial crime, sanctions monitoring, internal auditing and the units responsible for deciding whether risky clients stay or go.

When Christian Sewing became the chief executive of Deutsche Bank in 2018, after a string of scandals had tainted the bank’s reputation, he promised that the institution would be different: more stable and “a bit more boring.”

The bank has since spent years trying to convince the world that its era of scandals is over. The Inside Deutsche Bank project severely tests that narrative, laying bare a bank that built an enormous compliance machinery but repeatedly struggled to make it work.

The leak, provided via two whistleblowers, was shared with Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. Barracuda Media, a non-profit vehicle, was established to analyse the data and share it with reporters from more than 50 global media outlets spanning over 50 countries.

The whistleblowers, whose identities are being protected, copied the files and removed them from the institution. Besides giving them to Joseph and Sharife, they also provided material to the US Department of Justice, the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, and the UK’s HM Revenue and Customs, their lawyer confirmed.

It is evident that the whistleblowers wanted to expose Deutsche Bank’s relationships with both Russian oligarchs and Russian money.

“We are deeply committed to serving the public interest,” they said in a statement. They said the public has a right to know about the bank’s misconduct and its extensive banking of oligarchs. According to one of the whistleblowers, they believed the files contained potential criminal misconduct regarding business relationships with corrupt regimes.

The files show Deutsche Bank repeatedly missed warning signs of possible money laundering and sanctions violations. It bent its own rules for powerful clients. It allowed business considerations to override its own compliance regime. Sometimes, the bank only discovered serious failures years after suspicious money had passed through its systems.

The files also expose the intimate financial information of extremely powerful people.

Deutsche Bank accepted Epstein as a client in 2013, years after his conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor. The leak shows the bank later identified nearly $600 million in suspicious transactions involving him and his network — more than twice the amount previously publicly known.

Besides Trump and Epstein, who both famously used Deutsche Bank after other institutions shied away, the leak holds extensive details on Vladimir Putin-allied oligarchs like Oleg Deripaska and Roman Abramovich.

Deutsche Bank’s clients included a company whose ultimate beneficial owner was a Saudi businessman named on the famous “Golden Chain” list of purported sponsors of Al-Qaeda. And as a third-party correspondent bank, Deutsche Bank helped process payments linked to the late Rifaat al-Assad, Syria’s former vice-president known as the Butcher of Hama for his role in a bloody 1982 crackdown in the Syrian city.

In 2015, despite mounting adverse media reports and its own suspicious activity reports, or SARs, surrounding Jho Low, Deutsche Bank continued to process millions in transfers linked to the Malaysian financier.

Low is a central figure in the 1MDB scandal in which more than $4.5 billion was allegedly stolen from Malaysia’s state investment fund and laundered through global banks. Deutsche Bank’s Malaysian entity Deutsche Bank (Malaysia) Berhad is now being sued by 1MDB over its alleged role in moving part of these funds.

On the al-Assad payments, Deutsche Bank said:

“This matter has been resolved in 2022, as publicly disclosed. In the investigation proceedings of the public prosecutor’s office in Frankfurt in connection with two suspicious activity reports (SAR) filed by Deutsche Bank in the correspondent banking business, the bank accepted a fine of €7.01 million. The administrative penalty notice contains the allegations that the SARs were submitted too late because they should have been made in 2017 already. The bank cooperated in the proceedings.”

Deutsche Bank did not respond to questions about the individual on the Golden Chain list. The individual, who is identified in bank files only by his initials, was identified by reporters but did not respond to a request for comment.

Deripaska did not respond to requests for comment. Trump did not respond to a request for comment. Low could not be reached for comment.

A law firm representing Abramovich told reporters it is “not for our client to comment on Deutsche Bank’s internal processes and decisions.”

“To the extent those internal processes documented unfounded speculation concerning our client, he rejects that speculation,” they added. “He denies any allegation or suggestion of wrongdoing, including any allegation of criminal conduct, corruption or impropriety.”

The bank said: “We do not comment on potential, former or existing client relationships.”

On Epstein, the bank said it “acknowledges its error of onboarding Epstein in 2013 and regrets our historical connection with him. We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies and the US Congress regarding their investigations and have been transparent in addressing these matters in parallel.”

In a response to the wide range of topics raised in the leak, Deutsche Bank said matters raised by reporters “date back many years, in some cases decades. Where relevant, the bank said, these matters were reviewed at the time and were discussed with regulators and competent authorities as necessary.

“We are a different bank today,” the bank added. “Under Christian Sewing’s leadership, Deutsche Bank has gone through a fundamental transformation.”

The bank said it had invested 7 billion euros in its control environment between 2019 and 2025, supported by significant technology investments.

“These investments have been accompanied by a reinforced approach to identify and manage risks and a fundamental shift in culture. This work has supported the remediation of legacy issues and the completion of significant regulatory milestones.”

“Our progress has been recognised by the market, key regulators and supervisory authorities, as well as clients and other stakeholders. We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity.”

Over the coming weeks, the Inside Deutsche Bank media partners will publish many more stories drawn from the files. The files hold the secrets a major global bank is meant to keep confidential, unless it wants to lose its clients’ trust. Now, those secrets are out.

Deutsche Bank has paid more than 20 billion euros in fines and settlements since the year 2000 over identified failures related to mortgage securities, interest-rate manipulation, Russian mirror trades, anti-money-laundering failures, and other misconduct. Its reputation at one point became so toxic that, according to one internal account, BMW billionaire heiress Susanne Klatten declined an invitation from the bank, citing its poor reputation. Klatten denied refusing any such invitation from the bank, or that she ever used such terms in relation to the bank.

Now, the Inside Deutsche Bank investigation raises the question of whether one of the world’s largest financial institutions — deemed “too big to fail” after the 2008 financial crisis — is too broken to be able to fix itself. The bank operates across roughly 55 countries directly, and more than 140 countries are reached by its correspondent banking network.

Though the bank told reporters it is a “different bank today,” the leaked files show it has not become “boring” by any stretch of the imagination since Sewing took the helm.

In one case never before made public, the leak shows that in 2019 employees found what they believed to be a sprawling money laundering network that had moved hundreds of millions of euros, using the bank’s systems, through companies in Cyprus, Britain, Hong Kong and Ukraine.

The bank’s monitoring systems had detected pieces of the puzzle, but missed the big picture. It took roughly three years before one employee spotted the pattern, leading a manager to joke that the bank had found another “employee of the month.” The manager soon made a more important observation: “Our systems explicitly failed to detect it.”

In a response, the bank said it “takes its anti-financial crime and sanction-related obligations extremely seriously.” It said it “reviews potentially unusual activity, reports matters to the relevant authorities where required, and cooperates with lawful requests for information.”

In Colombia the bank’s own internal investigation, dubbed Project Cali, showed that in 2019 it had processed thousands of transactions for companies linked to the adult entertainment business. The money had been sent to women in Colombia through suspicious paths without the bank reporting most of the transactions to authorities.

The internal investigation flagged at least eight companies for “money laundering,” and another as “organised crime.” When the bank finally spotted the red flags it had missed across 2019, it filed 230 SARs and prohibited all payments from those companies. By that point, millions had already been transacted.

In a response on Project Cali, Deutsche Bank said it was “a historical review that led to specific remediation measures and a broader reassessment of financial-crime risks across Deutsche Bank’s correspondent- banking portfolio.”

“Decisions on suspicious-activity reporting are governed by jurisdiction-specific legal and confidentiality requirements, and we therefore cannot comment on individual reports, transactions, entities or counterparties.”

Reporters also found that beginning in 2015 Deutsche Bank facilitated transactions worth hundreds of millions of dollars involving the Singapore-based Xangbo group without spotting, or acting on, warning signs of suspicious activity.

These included transactions, made via Deutsche Bank’s Singapore branch, between Deutsche Bank’s Xangbo group clients and three companies accused of laundering alleged kickbacks for the Gupta brothers, who have been implicated in massive corruption and state capture in South Africa.

The Gupta-linked companies were allowed to move about $675 million between December 2012 and January 2017 through the Xangbo network, continuing even as South Africa erupted in public protests over the scandal that implicated the brothers. Of these movements, 30 pairs of transactions totalling $167 million were carried out across multiple accounts, often being done within a day.

It took an external whistleblower’s December 2019 allegations about unrelated, allegedly fraudulent activity in Singapore and elsewhere to finally nudge Deutsche Bank to further examine Xangbo’s transactions in more depth. Even then, records show the bank did not begin the process of exiting its relationship with Xangbo until 2021. Records further show the bank decided there were “no reasonable grounds” to file a report about a suite of convoluted transactions involving Xangbo.

In a response, Xangbo told reporters its accounts at the bank were not closed because of any dealings the group had with the Gupta-linked companies. “That is absolutely false,” a spokesperson said, adding that Deutsche Bank “continued to be our prime broker till 2022.”

The Guptas did not respond to a request for comment. They have previously said allegations against them are politically motivated.

In a response, Deutsche Bank said reporters’ findings on its dealings with Xangbo contained “several inaccuracies.” The bank said it would not comment on potential, former or existing client relationships, or on “actual or potential suspicious activity reporting.”

Meanwhile, reporters found that transactions involving suspected North Korean front companies went undetected even though some payment information contained the words “North Korea.”

“As a matter of policy, Deutsche Bank restricted dealing with North Korea and engaged with law enforcement and our regulators, as required,” the bank told reporters.

Room to manoeuvre

Sometimes, reporters found, the problem wasn’t incompetence — it was the bank’s appetite for business.

In one leaked email Sewing, who was then a member of the management board, complained that know-your-customer or KYC rules — the basic requirement that banks understand who their clients are, and where their money comes from — were affecting the bottom line. KYC bricht uns das revenue Genick, he wrote. KYC is breaking the back of our revenue.

In a response, the bank said it strongly rejects what it called “false insinuations” about Sewing’s “alleged attitude.”

It added: “Christian Sewing always emphasised that controls and risk management must be taken seriously and set as boundaries for the business. His focus on strong controls and risk management builds on a career during which he worked across all three lines of defence, spending the majority of the time in control functions.”

A recurring tension runs through the leak: People charged with controlling risk were repeatedly met with people paid to generate revenue. Amid this clash, powerful customers often had room to manoeuvre.

Take Timur Kulibayev, the billionaire son-in-law of Kazakhstan’s former president. Files show the bank acknowledging “historical concern as to the legitimacy of (Kulibayev’s) original source of wealth.”

In internal documents which identify Kulibayev as a bank “client” since as far back as 2006, it is also pointed out that in 2013, a risk analysis commissioned by the bank on Kulibayev had “highlighted a number of corruption allegations” stretching back to the early 2000s.

The bank’s anti-financial-crime department noted that he had not been convicted of corruption, and that one of his companies had provided evidence to show that criminal investigations into him in Europe had been dropped.

Yet after Kulibayev provided insufficient explanation for a January, 2020 “inflow” of $15 million into his account from a United Arab Emirates account, files show Deutsche Bank blocked the incoming funds.

Records indicate that weeks later, employees began the process of opening a Deutsche Bank account in Luxembourg under his wife’s name. Only months after that point did the bank discuss the possibility of ending the long relationship.

Kulibayev, via his law firm, denied any wrongdoing. The law firm said the bank had been made aware of his sources of income, which derived primarily from a joint ownership, with his wife, of the investment firm Almex and its shareholding in Halyk Bank of Kazakhstan.

A statement added: “Any suggestion therefore that Mr Kulibayev (or individuals working for him) concealed his source of wealth from Deutsche Bank, or knowingly provided false or misleading information about it, is categorically false.”

The law firm said Kulibayev was unable to identify the $15 million transaction based on the information provided. It added that any suggestion Kulibayev had personally banked with Deutsche Bank in the mid-2000s was false, and he “did not open a personal account until many years later.” It said reporters were appearing to “conflate the distinct personal and corporate banking relationships maintained by Mr Kulibayev and his businesses.”

Deutsche Bank said it does “not comment on actual, potential or former client relationships.”

Elsewhere, the bank can be seen choosing not to conduct a formal sanctions-risk review for subsidiaries of Bombardier, the Canadian aerospace and defence company, despite internal references to Bombardier’s doing business in prohibited, “special risk” countries. The justification given for the decision to instead perform an “informal” review included Deutsche Bank’s long relationship with the company. Bombardier revenues from these high-risk countries, it was pointed out, were low.

Bombardier did not respond to a request for comment.

The leak also exposes the flexibility of the bank’s hiring processes.

It recruited the children of influential politicians, executives and government officials, including applicants who failed aptitude tests or lacked qualifications. Alexey Storchak, the son of Russia’s deputy finance minister, was hired in 2010 and subsequently supplied colleagues with non-public information surrounding a bond issuance. As a result, files show Deutsche Bank itself subsequently investigated whether the bank itself should have ever possessed such information.

In 2019, the bank paid $16.1 million in a settlement after the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigated its hiring program. An internal calculation contained in the leak found that the bank generated roughly $190 million in revenues from transactions linked to the hiring of relatives of foreign government officials.

Storchak did not respond to a request for comment.

‘Good and bad oligarchs’

Russia, and the bank’s dealings with it, were among the whistleblowers’ primary concerns when contacting reporters with their information.

After Putin annexed Crimea in 2014, Western sanctions forced banks to decide which Russian clients were still palatable. “We started making lists,” a former Deutsche Bank insider told reporters. “Good and bad oligarchs.”

The leaked documents show the bank repeatedly facilitating sanctioned or politically exposed Russians, and remaining reluctant to fully abandon its long Russian entanglement. Documents show that by May 2020, with expansion of certain Russian business being planned by bank leaders, the move was described by one anti-financial-crime specialist as akin to throwing her team in front of a train.

Russia has continued to haunt the bank; early this year, German investigators searched Deutsche Bank’s Frankfurt headquarters in an investigation involving transactions reportedly associated with the oligarch Abramovich.

In a response, lawyers representing Abramovich said they had been instructed, “that the German authorities confirmed to our client that he is not under investigation in connection with the search of Deutsche Bank’s premises by the German Federal Criminal Police Office in January 2026.”

“Neither the German authorities nor Deutsche Bank has referred to our client (whether directly or indirectly) in any public statement about the searches, or indicated that any allegation is being made against him.”

Through correspondent banking, the invisible plumbing of global finance, Deutsche Bank moves money for other banks, giving them access to euros, dollars and international markets. It is lucrative and exceptionally difficult to police, and the underlying customers may be several steps removed from Deutsche Bank itself. Criminals, sanctioned entities and shell companies can disappear inside millions of ostensibly legitimate transactions.

Can a bank reliably identify money laundering, drug trafficking and human smuggling within such a system?

“No,” said Ulrich Göres, former head of Deutsche Bank’s anti-financial crime department. Why do banks do it? “For banking for high risk countries, and for high risk industries generally, higher fees can be charged.”

In one of its biggest scandals to date, Deutsche Bank was a major correspondent bank for Danske Bank’s Estonian branch. Roughly 200 billion euros flowed through Danske Bank’s Estonian branch between 2007 and 2015, much of it involving customers from Russia and other former Soviet states. Deutsche Bank helped process international payments for the branch as a correspondent bank.

In 2020, German authorities fined the bank 13.5 million euros for failing to promptly report suspicious transactions.“ Such penalties are a weak deterrent, Göres said, unless the penalty payments exceed the income generated previously.

On correspondent banking, Deutsche Bank said:

“Over the past decade, Deutsche Bank has substantially reduced its risk profile in this business, including exiting high-risk clients and countries. At the same time the bank has materially strengthened its financial crime controls and expertise … to manage the inherently elevated financial-crime risk in correspondent banking through significant investments.”

Junta warnings

Like its hiring practices, the bank’s climate aspirations proved flexible.

In 2020, Deutsche Bank promised it would no longer finance new oil and gas projects in the Arctic. Months later, it processed a 1.5 billion-euro payment connected to commodities giant Trafigura’s investment in the Arctic Vostok Oil project. The internal reasoning: Deutsche Bank was merely processing the transaction on behalf of Trafigura, they were not financing it themselves.

In a response Trafigura, which withdrew from the Vostok Oil project in 2022, confirmed the $1.5 billion transaction, made via Deutsche Bank, had taken place. Deutsche Bank did not directly address questions regarding Trafigura.

After Sewing publicly committed Deutsche Bank to a net-zero future in 2021, bankers pursued major Russian gas and petrochemical projects. When industrial chemicals multinational Linde sought the bank’s support for a huge gas complex in Ust-Luga, Russia, internal experts raised financial-crime, reputational and environmental concerns.

The head of trade finance had a different priority. “Super important and we must win this.” The deal was approved.

In a response, Linde said it holds itself accountable for the environmental performance of its operations “through clear targets and transparent reporting.”

A statement added: “In response to the invasion (of Ukraine) and the impact of global sanctions, Linde deconsolidated its Russian industrial gases and engineering business entities as of June 30, 2022; the company has operated in strict compliance with all applicable global sanctions and ceased any involvement in the Ust-Luga project.”

Deutsche Bank said the suggestion that it “sought to circumvent or avoid applying its sustainability framework is incorrect. The bank applies its policies and governance processes to transactions and client activities in accordance with the standards applicable at the relevant time.”

It added: “At the time the Ust-Luga LNG project was initiated, the relevant counterparties were not prohibited under applicable sanctions.” It said the transaction “was subject to the bank’s established environmental and reputational risk review processes.”

In Myanmar, the bank’s dealings have also raised concerns.

External advocates including a group of US senators warned in 2021 that business dealings between multinational energy companies and Myanmar’s state energy company MOGE could indirectly support the military junta.

Yet Deutsche Bank emails indicate it approved an increase in a guarantee to energy giant Halliburton for work in Myanmar shortly before the European Union sanctioned MOGE in February 2022. Records show the guarantee was to cover Halliburton’s services that were provided to an oil field project that was partly owned by MOGE.

Halliburton did not respond to a request for comment. Deutsche Bank did not directly address questions related to Halliburton, Myanmar and MOGE.

‘New Order’

When Trump won his first presidential term on Nov 8, 2016, Deutsche Bank faced an almost unprecedented situation: the president-elect was also one of its most controversial borrowers. The bank created a special project around him, codenamed “Novus Ordo.” New Order.

Trump-related documents were secured. Access was restricted. Communications were encrypted. Personal contacts minimised. But there was a larger problem: Trump and his businesses still wanted things from Deutsche Bank, like changes to existing loans.

The relationship had already gone spectacularly wrong once. After Trump failed to repay a loan for his Chicago tower during the financial crisis, he sued Deutsche Bank for $3 billion, essentially blaming it for a crisis that had damaged his business (the case was settled before trial). Deutsche Bank continued doing business with him.

And then came Russia.

As American prosecutors examined alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election, leading Democrats in the US Congress wanted to know whether Russians had guaranteed Trump’s Deutsche Bank loans, and whether Trump-related entities had ever raised wider money-laundering concerns.

The bank conducted an extensive internal review. It was not aware, according to an internal email prepared by its New York branch in 2019, “of any Bank-related links between President Trump and Russia related to Mr. Trump’s business with Deutsche Bank.”

But a 2020 memo from Brian Hagerty, then the bank’s director of its US financial crimes intelligence unit, references transactions connected to two Trump companies named DT Marks Baku LLC and THC Baku Services LLC. Both companies are listed as owned by Trump in his 2015 financial disclosure report filed with the US Office of Government Ethics.

Hagerty could not be reached for comment.

The memo stated that neither company were Deutsche Bank customers. But transactions involving the companies had raised internal concerns over potential links to the Azerbaijani and Russian laundromats, two notorious money laundering schemes.

The Hagerty memo notes that in 2018, a transaction between THC Baku Services LLC and “an entity reportedly associated to the Russian Laundromat scheme” was “included in a SAR.”

Deutsche Bank would not comment on Trump. It said in general terms, “banks are legally prohibited from commenting on their discussions with supervisory authorities in the US and on Suspicious Activity Reports, including their existence or non-existence.”

Reporters also found that by 2017, with Trump well into his first term, a Deutsche Bank employee accidentally sent an outside party a link containing financial information for 1,586 customers. Three accounts allegedly belonged to the newly-inaugurated president; these were called “DT” and “DJT” internally.

Managers debated whether Trump had to be informed of the leak, but concluded he did not. One manager called it a “brilliant outcome.” Sewing approved the case’s handling with a simple, “Ok.”

Heightened scrutiny

The Inside Deutsche Bank leak comes at a particularly sensitive time for an institution already under heightened scrutiny. This year alone, its offices have been raided at least four times, and the bank has filed several self-disclosures with authorities, according to a source with insight into the investigation.

Amid this mounting pressure, the leak offers an unprecedented glimpse into what has been going on behind closed doors. Trump. Epstein. Deripaska. Abramovich. Jho Lo. Even Thailand’s King Rama X, who did not respond to a request for comment, was a client. The list of major names, and global corporations, in the leak is enormous.

For many of these clients, the story is not about any of their own misconduct. It is that Deutsche Bank possessed highly sensitive information about their finances, families, companies and internal risk classifications, and that this information escaped.

The bank itself had anticipated the danger.

After a much smaller incident involving misdirected customer information in 2021, an employee warned that specialised law firms might see a potential business model in suing the bank over data breaches. Soon, the employee predicted, customers would be able to find standard legal claims online and copy them “1:1”.

The Inside Deutsche Bank leak is of an entirely different magnitude.

Potential lawsuits are only one threat. Regulators may examine the bank’s data security and compliance systems. With material now in the hands of US authorities, they can search huge troves of files for conduct they did not previously know about. Customers can decide whether they still trust the bank with their secrets.

The most damaging takeaway from the Inside Deutsche Bank investigation may not be that the bank had no rules. In reality, it employed armies of compliance officers, built extensive monitoring systems, and repeatedly promised regulators that it had, in fact, learned from past failures.

But those rules collided with big business.

Again and again, the files show the same sequence: a warning appears, compliance teams raise concerns, executives debate risk, and the bank finds a reason to continue. Sometimes the client was an oligarch. Sometimes the business involved a sanctioned market or a lucrative energy project. Sometimes, the bank’s systems simply failed to notice what was happening at all.

For years, Deutsche Bank decided what regulators, customers and the public could see. That era is over.

More than 15 million internal files. Emails from senior executives. Secret risk assessments. Suspicious transaction reports. Private information about billionaires, oligarchs, politicians and royalty. Records involving Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein and sanctioned businessmen. Previously undisclosed companies linked to authoritarian regimes.


Together, they add up to the largest cache of internal documents ever leaked to journalists from within a bank.


For months, more than 200 reporters from around the world examined the huge cache as part of an investigation called Inside Deutsche Bank. The records span some of the bank’s most sensitive functions and activities: anti-financial crime, sanctions monitoring, internal auditing and the units responsible for deciding whether risky clients stay or go.

news.title: Pete Buttigieg Brings Receipts to Torch Trump’s Airport Chaos Spin
news.text:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has fired back at President Donald Trump after the 80-year-old blamed him for the weekend’s air traffic disaster.

Buttigieg replied on X to a clip of Trump saying he “ruined” the air traffic control system during his tenure in the Biden administration.

“Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday. “What [the Democrats] did really set back the system a long way.” Trump’s rant was followed by a series of critical posts from the USDOT’s Rapid Response team on X.

“As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived,” the 44-year-old wrote on Monday. “We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in years.”

He continued, “As part of that work, I launched a project to transition the FAA’s communications system from copper wire to a modern network. I am glad the Trump administration has continued that work, but they have so far failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century.”

“I support more funding for FAA upgrades, but this episode is another blow to the public’s confidence that the administration can deliver,” Buttigieg wrote. “The Trump administration owes Americans an honest accounting of how they have spent the billions of dollars already authorized, clearer answers on why their repair work brought down the entire system on Friday, and an explanation of what they are doing to make sure this failure is not repeated.”

In response to Buttigieg’s statement, a White House spokesperson told the Daily Beast: “In 2023, in their own FAA report, it said over 100 of the agency’s tech systems were unsustainable. Despite that dire warning, the Biden DOT did nothing.”

Trump has taken heat for a series of major national outages over the past few days, starting with Microsoft’s service outage on Thursday, when millions of Americans lost access to the tech giant’s online services, including Outlook, Teams, and its AI agent Copilot.

The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued an unprecedented national ground stop, bringing domestic air travel to a standstill and complicating flight schedules for the next few days.

The president told reporters outside the White House on Monday that he takes “no responsibility” for the incident, instead praising Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and boasting that “everybody was safe, nobody was hurt.”

Later on Monday, thousands of Americans reported issues accessing their online accounts with banks including Chase, Wells Fargo, and J.P. Morgan.

That was followed by another major disruption on Monday evening, when United Airlines reported a “widespread system outage.”

The commercial airline said in a statement that it was “troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights.” United later announced after about 1.5 hours that the issue was resolved, adding that there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue,” according to the Associated Press.

news.title: Fox Host Goes Into Full Meltdown Over Travel Chaos
news.text:
Fox News pundit Jesse Watters melted down in a bizarre tirade following a series of flight outages affecting the country.

On The Five on Monday, the 48-year-old told viewers that he is stockpiling supplies amid the air travel chaos and that his family is now ready for war with Canada or an alien invasion.

Watters made the comments as he and the rest of The Five discussed the national ground stop that interrupted thousands of flights over the weekend.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered an hours-long nationwide ground stop Friday after technical problems disrupted air traffic control communications and radar systems. Airlines struggled to reposition aircraft and crews over the weekend, leaving thousands of flights canceled or delayed and hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded. The issues continued into Monday.

“This is a great dry run for maybe something that does happen. Say there’s an alien invasion. Say we go to war with Canada. The country has to remain calm and stick to a plan,” Watters said.

“I now have a family plan, and we’ve been stocking up. We now have weapons, we have bottled water and we have peanut butter.” 

Watters said his preparations would allow his family to survive 90 days off the grid, and urged viewers to make their own emergency plans.

Fox News did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Watters’ remarks. 

The Fox host has frequently jabbed at Canadian officials on-air, suggesting last year during an interview with Ontario Premier Doug Ford that Canadian citizens should consider President Donald Trump’s threats to annex their country a “privilege” because “everybody in the world” desires American citizenship. 

Watters had previously made similarly provocative remarks about the prospect of annexing Canada.

“The fact that they don’t want us to take them over, makes me want to invade,” Watters said in January 2025. “I want to quench my imperial thirst.” 

Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of making Canada the 51st U.S. state in recent months. 

In June, he reposted a Bloomberg article reporting that Canada had entered a technical recession in a Truth Social post with the caption, “51st state!” 

In September, during an interview with the New York Times, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested Trump’s rhetoric about potential annexation–even if less-than-serious–forced Canada to make military considerations about its neighbor to the south. 

“You have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney said. “So, and as the tail fattens when a leader of a country threatens your sovereignty, you adjust accordingly. That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to take certain things into consideration.”

news.title: Duffy vows to modernize aging air traffic system after nationwide ground stop
news.text: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday said he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America" following a nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded more than a million passengers. During an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," Duffy said he wants to build a brand-new modern architecture "of a resilient telecom network." "Congress did give me $12.5 billion. That’s for radar and radios. I am well on my way to deploying all that money. You can’t buy this off the shelf, so I’ve ordered it. As it is delivered, we pay for it, and we deploy it into the NAS. But what’s really important is the next phase of the investment," he told host Sean Hannity on Monday. The $12.5 billion in congressional funding is part of a broader effort to modernize the nation's air traffic control system, including communications, surveillance and other infrastructure. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' "So you saw a telecom issue on Friday. We’re replacing old copper wires with fiber, but this is an old architecture of a network. You’ve seen Newark go down. You’ve seen Dallas go down. You saw all of New York go down just a couple of months ago because of telecom issues. I want to build a brand-new architecture of a resilient telecom network that’s worthy of 2026 and worthy of America," he continued. Duffy added that the department needs new software. "The software we use to manage our airplanes in the airspace was built in the 1990s. It works. It works well. But if we’re going to drive more safety and more efficiency, we need brand-new software," he explained. The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence that a cyberattack forced the ground stop on Friday and that the Federal Aviation Administration was investigating whether a network problem, router issue or installation error caused the system failure. The FAA is working with contractor L3Harris, which installed the router in question and is assisting with the investigation at its Florida laboratory. "We had all of our intelligence agencies, at Donald Trump’s direction, talk on Friday night," Duffy said. "No one was seeing any kind of hack into our system. And we’ve now secured the router." BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We’re doing an analysis in Florida with L3Harris and the FAA. I actually asked the FBI to come in just to make sure, to put people at ease, that this was not a hack. So I think it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error," he continued. The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend.
news.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says Friday's FAA ground stop was no hack, as the FAA probes a router issue, network problem or installation error.

news.title: China stocks flat as chip curbs lift local tech, hit internet giants
news.text:
HONG KONG: Chinese stocks struggled to recover from multi-month lows on Tuesday as investors assessed the impact of tighter US restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips and awaited the APEC summit.

China’s blue-chip CSI300 index was up 0.05% at the midday break after dipping to thelowest since July 2025.

The Shanghai Composite index was nearly flat at 3,602.07 points, having slid as much as 1% earlier in the session to the lowest since August 2025.

Tech shares helped lift the broader market, with the startup board ChiNext Composite index 0.7% higher and Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR50 index up 3.3%.

The CSI Semiconductor Index rallied nearly 6% and the info tech sector added 2.6%, as investors bet the Trump administration’s further restriction on China’s access to advanced US AI chips could benefit local players.

Shares in Chinese internet giants, on the other hand, slid on concerns that the limited access to advanced chips would hinder their AI ambitions. Alibaba fell nearly 5%, while Baidu shed nearly 7%.

That dragged the broader Hong Kong market lower.

The Hang Seng Index was down 0.8% at 23,571.61, and the Hang Seng Tech Index lost 0.5%.

“We expect greater differentiation even within the same sector,” analysts at Morgan Stanley wrote in a note.

Further tech restrictions against China will strengthen the policy and demand case for domestic self-sufficiency plays, while increasing risks for offshore names that rely on US-licensed hardware or offshore computing capacity, they added.

Investors were also watching the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on November 18-19.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to hold a trilateral meetingto discuss global flashpoints, ranging from trade policy and the wars in Ukraine and Iran to nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence.

Elsewhere in Asia, markets followed Wall Street lower as US-China technology restrictions weighed on sentiment ahead of Nvidia’s earnings.

news.title: China taps US AI models to train homegrown rivals as chip curbs bite
news.text: Chinese entities are adopting increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals, documents show, as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and offset tightening US curbs on its access to chips.A Reuters review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices and government documents reveals how the practice - known as distillation - has expanded beyond academic experiments into mainstream industrial use in China.The records describe Chinese researchers using US models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models.The documents also show that Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across China's powerful manufacturing sector.Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world. While the process cannot reproduce a leading model's full capabilities or eliminate the need for advanced computing power, it can help developers preserve selected skills in smaller systems that cost less to operate, potentially reducing their reliance on American technology.China's broadening use of distillation could undercut the effectiveness of US curbs on the sale of advanced chips to China, as its developers can build AI capabilities by drawing on those of their American rivals. Washington said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to such chips from companies like Nvidia.Distillation is also a source of friction between the world's two biggest economies ahead of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are expected to meet.US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of aggressive, targeted distillation of American AI models on an industrial scale.And at meetings in Chengdu in July, US Commerce Department officials raised concerns with Chinese regulators about developers collecting output from leading American AI models, warning that some activities could amount to intellectual-property theft, three people familiar with the discussions said.Chinese officials defended distillation as a standard AI-development technique and said they were open to acting where the conduct constituted IP theft, but made no concrete commitments, according to a US official familiar with the previously unreported exchange.The US Commerce Department and China's Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment.FROM AMERICAN ANSWERS TO CHINESE MODELSDistillation involves a powerful 'teacher' model generating answers or demonstrating how to complete tasks, which developers use to train a smaller 'student' system.For Chinese developers facing constraints on computing power, the attraction is in making one expensive query do repeated work, according to a former Alibaba Group engineer who spoke on condition of anonymity. An American model can generate the answer to a difficult question once, allowing a Chinese team to retain useful examples and train a local system around them.In a November 2024 paper, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers described selecting about 5,000 answers from OpenAI's o1 model, translating them using GPT-4o mini and assembling 10,750 bilingual training examples to further train Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B model.The researchers also cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation, leaving developers dependent on breakthroughs made by more advanced model providers.The project illustrated how American model output can become reusable data, allowing developers to improve domestic systems without repeatedly consulting the original provider.Alibaba researchers described a more systematic approach in an April 2025 paper, using OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-4o to generate training material in languages other than Chinese, then refining and scoring responses before training smaller Qwen models.In a February 2026 paper, researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chinese food-delivery company Meituan described using GPT-4o to generate plans for coordinating AI agents working together on programming problems, helping train a smaller model to organise such tasks.Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment.A GROWING GEOPOLITICAL DISPUTEAmong leading American AI companies, OpenAI's terms restrict using its output to develop competing models, subject to exceptions, while Anthropic similarly restricts training competing systems without permission.A US official familiar with the July Chengdu regulatory discussions said Washington believes industrial-scale distillation is the main reason Chinese AI models have narrowed the gap with their American rivals.Two people familiar with Chinese developers' operations disputed that assessment, saying distillation was only one factor alongside advances in engineering, algorithms, data and model design.Chinese government documents do not instruct companies to distil American models but encourage distillation as part of Beijing's push to spread AI across the world's second-largest economy.A national AI+Manufacturing policy package published by eight Chinese government agencies in January includes guidance supporting model training, fine-tuning and distillation for industrial applications. Shanghai and Shenzhen have also encouraged techniques to reduce computing requirements.The policies reflect Beijing's ambition to deploy smaller, cheaper AI systems across industries.Concerned by distillation's growing geopolitical sensitivities, Chinese AI developers have in recent months asked Beijing's industry regulator for guidance on the boundaries between ordinary use of foreign models and organised collection of output for training, according to one person familiar with the discussions.China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to a request for comment.
news.summary: Chinese entities are adopting increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals, documents show, as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and offset tightening US curbs on its access

news.title: Trump suggests he will meet Kim Jong Un at summit in China with Putin and Xi
news.text:
US president Donald Trump has suggested that he will meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un this week on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation conference in China.

Mr Trump told reporters before departing the White House en route to the Philippines on Monday that any meeting would happen in China, and that the North Korean leader’s presence was ultimately up to Xi Jinping, the Chinese president.

“We may meet with Kim Jong Un,” Mr Trump told reporters before boarding Marine One. “We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”

Mr Trump met the North Korean leader three times during his first term and has previously expressed interest in a fourth meeting during his current term.

Senior US officials told said on Friday that there were no immediate plans for Kim to join the trilateral meeting already planned between Mr Xi, Mr Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Discussions are expected to focus largely on developing an ambitious nuclear arms-control pact, although a full deal to limit weapons is unlikely.

China, Russia and the US have the largest arsenals of nuclear weapons in the world. Russia and the US are estimated to hold around 83pc of all stockpiled weapons, with thousands of warheads each. China’s stockpile is much smaller, at around 620.

On Monday, the Kremlin said it was “hard to overestimate” the importance of the summit between the leaders of Russia, China and the US, scheduled for Thursday in Shenzhen.

“The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate,” Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said on Monday. He added that the meeting was based on a format taking into account “the mutual understanding and alliance between our countries” during World War II.

Beijing touted it as a chance to focus on “world peace”.

“They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said Mao Ning, China’s foreign ministry spokesman.

“Under the current circumstances, the three countries bear an important responsibility to co-operate in addressing global challenges and to promote world peace and stability.”

Europe and Ukraine fear Russia is set on pushing a so-called “new Yalta”, a reference to the 1945 meeting in Crimea between the leaders of the Soviet Union, US and the UK, which divided Europe into spheres of influence, setting the stage for the Cold War.

The decision by Putin to bring Mr Xi to the table to help with the negotiations is probably an effort to capitalise on the recent goodwill established between China and the US.

Putin is likely to be hoping that his Chinese counterpart can put pressure on the US to halt its remaining support for Ukraine.

Mr Trump told reporters on Monday that he thought Putin was “backing down” in the war on Ukraine, adding: “He could be a lot tougher, frankly.”

Putin proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war with Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported last month. However, officials said that Mr Trump is not expected to raise the issue during the trilateral meeting.

Olivia Wales, the White House’s assistant press secretary, told reporters: “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous.”

However, the elephant in the room will be the absence of Jensen Huang after his resignation as Nvidia chief executive. Mr Huang was by Mr Trump’s side during his trip to China in May and when Mr Xi visited the White House in September. 

The tech boss resigned in disgrace last week after the revelation of extramarital affairs with two employees and Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, the Asian tech firm. Beijing has called the US intelligence conclusions “smears and slanders”. As the head of the global tech company, Mr Huang heavily influenced US AI foreign policy.

The flow of Russian diesel and gas will also potentially be a point of discussion after Mr Trump ignored his own legislation and struck a deal with Putin in October to buy 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel.
news.author: Connor Stringer

news.title: Donald Trump backs calls for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO
news.text:
US president Donald Trump supported calls for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive officer and downplayed national security concerns about the ousted executive’s relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

“I would not mind that,” Mr Trump told reporters on Monday at the White House before leaving for his trip to Asia, when asked about the possibility of Mr Huang returning as CEO. 

“A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.”

Nvidia was down roughly 2pc in New York trading on Monday, though the shares had briefly turned positive as Mr Trump spoke.

Mr Huang has discussed the possibility of returning to his position with his confidants, the Financial Times reported on Monday. 

A “war room” of Silicon Valley executives is also being organised to lobby for Mr Huang and get the White House’s backing, the report said.

Mr Trump’s position puts him at odds with treasury secretary Scott Bessent, who called for a “dramatic shake-up” in Nvidia and an external search for new leadership.

Mr Trump also played down concerns that Mr Huang’s actions exposed the US to national security risks. 

“It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China,” the president said.

Mr Trump also cast doubts on allegations that Alice Huang — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International with whom Mr Huang admitted having an affair — was indeed working for the Chinese government.

“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy,” he said.

Mr Huang cultivated a close relationship with the president, enjoying the kind of access to the White House that few corporate leaders have had, even as the ousted CEO advocated for easing restrictions on US chip exports to China. 

The president has repeatedly defended Mr Huang since the scandal broke over his affair with Alice Huang.

In a social media post, investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a “slow, measured and deliberate” approach to Nvidia’s future leadership.

That should include “the potential return of Jensen Huang”, Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker wrote in a letter to Nvidia’s board posted on X. 

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, another Mr Huang ally, has also voiced his support for a comeback.

Mr Trump, who is travelling to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen later this week for a meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders, said he might raise allegations of Chinese spying on Nvidia with China’s president Xi Jinping when they meet on the summit’s sidelines. 

The president and his officials had earlier said he will not bring up the matter with his Chinese counterpart.

Beijing has denied the espionage claims and called them “purely a smear”.

news.title: Flooded Gaza needs ‘immediate’ aid, Board of Peace warns Israel
news.text:
Donald Trump’s Board of Peace has accused Israel of an “insufficient” response to deadly floods that have hit the Gaza Strip.

In a rare statement, the US-led body, charged with ending war in Gaza and rebuilding the strip, called on Israel “to act immediately to authorise and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterisation and humanitarian supplies”.

“The situation no longer represents simply a threat posed by the approaching winter, but an immediate humanitarian emergency,” it said on Monday.

The board has been pushing Israel for at least a month to speed up its “winterisation” policies so that residents in Gaza are better able to withstand the coldest months of the year.

The statement followed a weekend of torrential rain and winds that battered the decimated territory’s displacement camps, causing widespread flooding, landslides and several deaths.

A mother and her three young children were killed when a sand dune collapsed onto their tent in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza. The children, aged four, five and eight died on Sunday. Their mother also suffocated under the sand.

Some 350,000 people, including 210,000 children, were affected by the storm, according to estimates by Save the Children. More than 70,000 tents, as well as shelters, latrines and belongings, were damaged or destroyed after 12 hours of rain on Saturday.

Nearly half the population, about 950,000 people, are living in sites that are at risk of flooding, according to the Norwegian Refugee Council, which is leading the aid effort to provide shelter. 

More than 2,000 shaky war-damaged buildings are now also at risk of collapse, says Save the Children.

“Rain did not kill these children. They were killed by man-made conditions created by the Israeli authorities, forcing families to live in unsafe, inadequate shelters with nowhere else to go,” said Ahmad Alhendawi, regional director for the Middle East, at Save the Children International.

Footage on social media showed displaced Palestinians attempting to repair their damaged tents — often just tarpaulin propped up with poles — and cover gaps with plastic sheeting, as gushing torrents sweep household items away.

Tamer Nahed, a Palestinian journalist, said parents spent the entire night scooping their children above the filthy water that flooded their tents and drenched their mattresses. 

“They couldn’t find a single dry place to put their children. They couldn’t even give them a few hours of sleep,” he wrote on X. (© Telegraph Media Group Holdings Ltd)

news.title: US court strikes down visa rules restricting stays of foreign students, journalists
news.text:
A United States federal judge on Monday struck down a policy imposed by President Donald Trump that would impose stricter visa limits on how long international students and journalists can study or work in the US, AFP reported.

The ruling came from an appeal filed against the Department of Homeland Security by a coalition of unions representing universities, teachers and journalists.

The new rules that were announced in July were expected to impact international students with F visas, visitors on cultural exchange programmes who possess a J visa and foreign journalists with an I visa.

Under the proposed new rules, international students would be allowed to stay in the US for a maximum of up to four years after which they would have to apply for an extension. Previously, foreigners on student visas were allowed to stay for the entire duration of their studies.

The proposed rule also sought to shorten how long foreign journalists can stay in the country from up to five years to 240 days, or 90 days in case of Chinese journalists.

The grace period for students after completing their studies was also proposed to be reduced from 60 days to 30 days. During this time, students must leave the country, transfer to another institution or change to a different immigration status if they wish to remain in the US.

While dismissing the policy, Boston Judge Dennis Saylor said that it was “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law”, AFP reported. 

The new visa regulations had been scheduled to take effect in September but were temporarily put on hold by the bench. The Trump administration has already appealed against it in a higher court.

“Put bluntly, [The Department of Homeland Security] is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity – providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States – that Congress sought to permit and encourage,” the judge said.

He said the policy would “prohibit foreign students from engaging in extended periods of study, such as those required for PhD programs, prohibit them from obtaining joint degrees (and) prohibit them from changing their academic concentration”.

The programs that would have been affected by the new visa regulations have attracted heavy Indian enrolment, among the 3.31 lakh students from the country currently studying in the US.

In 2020, a similar proposal was announced at the end of Trump’s first term, but it was withdrawn by the Joe Biden administration in 2021.

As of 2024, there were about 1.6 million international students on F visas in the US.

In 2023-’24, the authorities granted 13,000 visas for journalists and more than 3.5 lakh J visas meant for cultural exchange visitors.

Since taking office in his second term in January 2025, Trump announced several measures as part of his immigration crackdown.

Edited by Sara Varghese.
