news.title: American Forensic Expert: Jeffrey Epstein Was Likely Murdered, Not Died by Suicide
news.text:
Professor Freeman did not personally examine Epstein's body, but he reviewed the forensic records concerning his death. Based on what he observed, he stated on a BBC broadcast that Epstein had been strangled—most likely with a ligature from behind, the BBC reports.

At the same time, the medical examiner who performed the autopsy on Epstein's body seven years ago issued an official conclusion that the nature of the injuries was consistent with suicide. He also concluded that there were no wounds on the body typically sustained by someone fighting off an attacker.

The 66-year-old Jeffrey Epstein, who was friends with numerous politicians and prominent business figures from the US, the UK, and other countries, including Donald Trump, was found dead on August 10, 2019, in a cell in a New York prison. He was held there awaiting trial on charges of sexual exploitation of underage girls.

New York's Chief Medical Examiner at the time, Dr. Barbara Sampson, who concluded that Epstein's death was a suicide, previously stated: "I stand firmly behind our determination regarding the cause and manner of Mr. Epstein's death. The cause is hanging, the manner is suicide."

Throughout his career, Michael Freeman has worked as a forensic expert for attorneys general across various US states, determining the causes of death in custody or detention, including the death of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020.

He received the medical examination documents of Epstein's body from Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, studied them over the course of a year, and on Monday presented a report on his findings at University College London. He then discussed his conclusions on a BBC broadcast.

What Freeman specifically says

Mark Epstein himself is convinced that his brother was murdered.

Professor Freeman insists that he reviewed the documents impartially and that Mark Epstein did not pay him anything. His study has not been peer-reviewed by other experts.

Freeman told the BBC that, in his view, the evidence suggests Epstein was attacked. Among this evidence is severe bruising on the left shoulder and injuries that could indicate a blow to the face.

According to Professor Freeman, the results of the post-mortem examination point with a high probability to ligature strangulation using an improvised garrote, followed by the suspension of the body on the bunk bed using the same ligature.

He said that fingernail scratch marks could be seen above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck.

"This is consistent with ligature strangulation, especially from behind, and the victim's attempts to pull the ligature off the neck," the forensic expert explained.

"The injuries and the position in which the body was found are inconsistent with one another. So that leaves only one explanation: the death was the result of homicide," Professor Freeman stated.

The medical examiner who performed Epstein's autopsy told the US Department of Justice that Epstein's injuries were more consistent with suicide by hanging than homicide by strangulation. He also noted the absence of defensive wounds that might have appeared while the victim was defending himself (injuries often found on strangulation victims).

Furthermore, according to Freeman, in the case of a death by hanging in prison, he would have expected investigators to provide a photograph of the body taken before it was removed from the ligature.

The US Department of Justice, following an investigation into the circumstances of Epstein's death, stated that the guard who found Epstein hanging immediately called a colleague, and together they laid the body on the floor and attempted CPR.

In addition, the Department of Justice stated that a month before his death, Epstein had briefly been placed on suicide watch over concerns that he might take his own life.

When asked who could have killed Epstein, Dr. Freeman replied: "I have no idea. I have no opinion on that. That was not at all the objective of my investigation."

In response to a question about whether his views could be seen as bordering on conspiracy theories, the expert stated: "Fortunately, I can say: don't take my word for it, let everyone examine the available evidence for themselves."

"If you think I'm peddling conspiracy theories because I look at something that resembles strangulation and call it strangulation rather than hanging, show me where I'm wrong," the expert continued. "I am completely open to that. I am a scientist; I am always glad to hear reasoned opinions from other people."

Jeffrey Epstein was first accused of soliciting minors for prostitution in 2008, but back then, thanks to a plea agreement, he received only 13 months in prison.

Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with orchestrating a vast network of sexual exploitation of underage girls, facing decades in prison under those charges.

news.title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
news.text: TAIPEI: Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island's biggest informal ally and seller of arms."For the Trump administration, this isn't a core issue between the U.S. and China," said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan's Central Police University.US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenesExperts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump's public ambivalence toward Taiwan.One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity."This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised," said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion..Elon Musk expected to accompany Trump on China visit; Iran on agenda for trilateral talks with Xi, Putin.The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island's relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don't."I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers," said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. "I think Taiwan's importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine."Stalled arms sales for nowSince starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low."I don't think this is a political issue. They just can't produce so many of these missiles in a short period," he said..China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss 'world peace'.China expands coast guard role in pressure on TaiwanMeanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People's Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan's Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan's National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025."I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off" Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China's claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan's east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan's outlying islands closer to China.Wang compared the approach to Beijing's tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection."It's telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.".Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: US to close AI chip loophole after Nvidia scandal
news.text:
The United States announced tougher export controls on AI chips on Monday after a scandal involving Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang exposed a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.

The news came the day before Californian chip titan Nvidia reports its first earnings since Huang’s departure as CEO, with investors questioning if the artificial intelligence boom can hold strong.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

These changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.

While this loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Nvidia co-founder Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive of Megaspeed — a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of export controls.

Jensen Huang, 63, stepped down last week after at least two extramarital affairs were revealed in media reports.

Facing criticism, the US Commerce Department said Monday it would close a loophole that had drawn concern from US authorities.

The move “is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement.

It weighed on Nvidia’s shares, which shed four percent on Monday, extending a slide since the scandal erupted.

• ‘Business-as-usual’ unlikely –

Nvidia stock has lost more than a quarter of its value over the past month, as doubts grow about the health of the AI investment boom.

Tuesday’s results will be the first presented under chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.

“If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer, describing the company as in turmoil.

Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.

Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy — with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday.

Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty.

• ‘Trusted access’ –

On Tuesday, Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures.

The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said.

Indonesia said it was reviewing the measure “and seeking industry input on its potential impact on operations and investment, including in the data centre sector”.

The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an investigation into Jensen Huang’s dealings with Megaspeed, and accuses the Commerce Department of ignoring widespread reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China.

Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors are meanwhile gathering signatures for an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

“The most important time to help someone is when they’re down,” investor Bill Ackman said at a Semafor tech conference.

Before leaving for summits in Asia, President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, waving off the security concerns.

But given the legal cloud over him, most Wall Street analysts doubt that the AI rock star can return anytime soon.

Kress, a non-engineer, is not expected to stay in the role permanently, leaving Nvidia facing a high-stakes search for a successor.
news.summary:
The United States announced tougher export controls on AI chips on Monday after a scandal involving Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang exposed a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.

news.title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
news.text:
On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.

Ríos was happy to share.

With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy.

“It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said.

Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes: a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand. 

Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state. Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory.

But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility.

“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.” 

Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems, electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers.

As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico, proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities.

“There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans.

 A solar revolution after Hurricane Maria 

The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths.

“We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.”

There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout.

“The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer.

Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage. 

In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate.

If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available.

The experiment has faced challenges. In a 2026 survey of solar customers by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors, some participants criticized the compensation structure, which varies by solar provider. Others expressed hesitation to enroll in the program because they did not understand it or feared losing backup power.

Ríos said he’s only had that problem once — when a storm knocked out power right after he shared his battery. He now skips battery sharing events if there's bad weather forecast. 

He acknowledged the payment system is “a little vague.” He and his wife received $162 last year, which they happily redeemed as a Marshalls gift card. 

Luma told The Associated Press that relying so often on battery sharing has contributed in part to recent rate increases. The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.

Rúa Jovet says that expense doesn’t compare to the societywide economic losses of frequent power outages that spoil food, endanger health and shutter schools and businesses. The territory is also set to spend more than $1.7 billion this year importing fuel for most of its power generation. 

 Creating a consistent energy source 

Luma said each battery sharing event, typically about four hours, supports the equivalent of about 80,000 residential customers. Enrolling more households would enable supplemental power for more hours.

But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger. 

“The VPP in Puerto Rico is like an emergency escape valve, but the batteries should be a grid asset,” said Jigar Shah, director of the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office under former President Joe Biden and comanaging director of the advisory firm Multiplier.

Instead of only being tapped in an emergency, Shah said, the batteries could dispatch power every day — offsetting the need to burn fossil fuels — and help absorb excess energy across the grid when solar panels are producing at their peak. Several states, including California and Texas, use solar and batteries this way.

VPPs “could potentially play a larger role in Puerto Rico’s energy future,” Alejandro Figueroa, Luma chief regulatory officer, told The Associated Press. But, he said, a program used daily would require a different design and compensation structure to be sustainable.

Providing daily power is a natural next step, Rúa Jovet said, and could help Puerto Rico meet its own legal mandate that the archipelago reach 100% renewable energy by 2050. But a virtual power plant alone cannot solve the territory’s energy crisis. 

That will require deploying billions of unspent federal recovery dollars, continuing improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure and building new large-scale generation and storage.

“You don’t want the situation to be a persistent emergency forever,” he said.

news.title: Kremlin Rejects US-China-Russia Meet's Comparison With 1945 Yalta Conference
news.text: The Kremlin on Monday dismissed as "games of political scientists" any suggestion that this week's meeting of the leaders of Russia, China and the United States was comparable to the 1945 Yalta conference which tried to set out the future of post-war Europe.The meeting on Thursday in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit with Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump has prompted comparisons to the talks between the wartime Soviet, British and US leaders that established great-power spheres of influence after World War Two.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected any such notion, saying at least two participants - Russia and China - stood for a "multi-polar world order" with no decisions imposed on other nations.READ | Nuclear Talks With Russia, China, Meet With Kim Jong Un: Trump's Asia Agenda"These are the games of political scientists and have nothing to do with reality," Peskov, quoted by Interfax news agency, told journalists."To say that someone or other intends to decide the fate of the world, this is definitely not Russia, definitely not China. We don't want anyone to decide our fate and will never try to decide the fate of others."He described the forthcoming talks as "a very important meeting and there has not been anything like it."Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing this would be the first face-to-face meeting among the heads of state of China, Russia, and the United States.READ | First Ever US-China-Russia Trilateral Summit On ThursdayShe gave no details on what would be on the agenda but said stronger communication among the three leaders "along with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries".Peskov said part of the meeting would be open to the media.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: The American Handshake Maintains Its Grip
news.text:
Despite the best efforts of Dr. Anthony Fauci and others, the American handshake survived COVID-19.

Calls to End the Custom

During the pandemic, Fauci and other public health officials tried to end all kinds of things they deemed unclean.

Self-serve buffets, shared restaurant menus and blowing out birthday candles were targeted as germ-spreading hazards whose time had come.

But few things agitated them as much as the American handshake.

In April 2020, Fauci, then director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, said that once our shuttered country reopened, the handshake had to go.

He told podcast host Kate Linebaugh on “The Journal” that ditching the handshake would prevent the spread of germs and “probably would decrease instances of influenza dramatically in this country.”

Fauci had a point. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Americans aren’t very good at washing their hands with soap and water — and unwashed hands are germ factories.

Other critics offered cultural reasons to end the custom.

In a 2020 piece for The Atlantic, staff writer Megan Garber called it a “terrible custom” that no longer made sense because, in addition to spreading germs, it often became a contest of dominance rather than a sign of equality.

CNN’s Chris Cillizza predicted the greeting was finished for gladhanding politicians — while health officials and etiquette coaches urged Americans to replace the handshake with waves, nods, fist bumps and elbow bumps.

In a Los Angeles Times editorial, the paper argued it is time to kill the handshake, an outdated relic whose risks outweighed its rewards.

More Than a Peace Treaty

According to History.com (“The History of the Handshake”), one popular theory is that the handshake began as a way of conveying peaceful intentions.

By extending their empty right hands, strangers could show they were not holding weapons and bore no ill will.

Greetings across cultures have long served to signal peaceful intent.

Whether it is a bow in Japan, pressing palms together in India or a handshake in the West, such greetings have long served as a social peace treaty.

Over the centuries, however, the handshake evolved beyond a survival gesture into the ultimate trust-building tool.

A HuffPost essay titled “The Power of a Handshake” noted that the gesture serves as a first step toward affiliation and the building of a bond with another person.

A firm handshake can improve hireability.

Research by University of Iowa management professor Greg Stewart, published in the Journal of Applied Psychology, found that a firm, confident handshake signals openness and trustworthiness and can influence hiring judgments in job interviews.

That has been my experience.

When someone greets me with a cold, clammy handshake and a weak grip, my impression is not positive.

When the grip is too tight and the eye contact too eager, I sense someone is trying too hard.

But when the grip is just firm enough — and the eye contact natural and confident — my trust begins immediately.

Here to Stay

Despite the predictions from experts, the American handshake has made a full COVID-19 recovery.

Paleoanthropologist Ella Al-Shamahi, author of “The Handshake: A Gripping History,” saw the comeback coming all along.

In her 2021 book and in interviews promoting it, she dismissed premature obituaries for the greeting, calling it “one of the gold standards of human connection” and arguing that it is deep within our DNA.

Some are not happy about that.

In a 2026 piece for The Atlantic, writer Tom Bartlett complained about men who squeeze too hard to assert dominance — noting that this is the aggressive style favored by President Donald Trump.

Which is ironic.

Trump, a self-described germaphobe, wrote in his 1997 book that the handshake was “one of the curses of American society.” He called it “barbaric” in interviews and said in 2020 that people might stop shaking hands, noting he would not be upset if the custom ended.

But the good old American handshake isn’t going anywhere. Despite shifting fashions, it remains one of our most instinctive gestures.

You can shake on it.

news.text:
For many years I regularly watched Tucker Carlson Tonight on Fox News. Although Carlson’s preppy condescension could be annoying, I agreed with much of his commentary, enjoyed many of his guests, and he was a welcome reprieve during the dark and dismal Obama years. Carlson falsely charges that Israel drew the United States into war with Iran when, in fact, the United States independently decided to join with Israel in attacking Iran after Israel — as a strong and reliable ally — shared vital intelligence with the U.S. concerning the whereabouts of Iranian leadership. And Carlson even urged Michiganders to vote for the Marxist Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — the most repugnant Jew-hater to seek high public office in this country at least since the Holocaust — solely because of their deep common hatred of Jews.

In 2009, the preeminent American economist and author George Gilder published "The Israel Test," which postulated that a person’s attitude toward Israel revealed much about his or her character. The test, according to Gilder, is whether people and societies are prepared to learn from Israel’s remarkable success or are determined to undermine it.

I now propose a similar test: The Tucker Carlson Test. Any politician seeking my vote, and hopefully those of my fellow Jews and other supporters of Israel, must first loudly and clearly denounce Tucker Carlson for his vile Jew-hatred. No game-playing, no back-pedaling, and nothing two-faced: Carlson must be publicly condemned for hating Jews.

So what exactly do you want to “change,” Mr. Vice President? Should Israel no longer be our ally? Do you question Israel’s existence as the world’s only Jewish state?

So, Mr. Vice President: If this is not an accurate characterization of your political motivation, then prove it by denouncing your longtime “friend.” To compete for my vote, you’ll have to ace the Tucker Carlson Test. I’m listening intently, Mr. Vice President — as are many of my right-minded fellow American Jews, Zionists, and other morally committed and clear-minded conservatives. Disappoint us at your own political peril.

news.title: White House Says ‘No Credible Threat’ After Iran Dirty Bomb Report
news.text: The White House told Newsweek there are currently "no credible threats" targeting the U.S. following a report that Iran is developing plans to potentially detonate a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. The CNN report, which cited seven U.S. officials, said the new intelligence points to a potential effort to target senior Trump administration officials. “We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to Newsweek on Monday. Sources familiar with the intelligence characterized the planning as an effort to give Iran options rather than an indication of an imminent attack. The report said officials remain divided over the credibility of the intelligence and whether Iran has the personnel in place to carry out such a plot. Newsweek reached out to Iran’s Mission to the United Nations for comment. A spokesperson for the mission told CNN that Tehran considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be “wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard.” The reported intelligence comes amid broader concerns of Iranian threats against senior U.S. officials. Newsweek reported last week that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had moved out of his Washington-area home and onto a military base following threats against his life from Iran. Bessent's relocation came as U.S. officials assessed that Iranian efforts to target current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage. He was the third Trump Cabinet member reported to have moved into military housing, following Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Reports have since indicated that Attorney General Todd Blanche has also been living at a military installation in the Washington, D.C., area for months. While speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, President Donald Trump was asked whether he was concerned about being targeted by Iranian drones. “I'm worried about you, because if they get me, you're gone too. Be careful,” Trump told the reporter. The president has sent mixed signals about the next steps in the war, at times threatening further military action against Iran while saying the conflict is “militarily...effectively over.” Last week, he warned that U.S. forces were “locked and loaded” and said Washington was monitoring Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran's nuclear program, for signs of activity. CNN senior national security reporter Katie Bo Lillis said U.S. officials are reportedly taking the new intel “very, very seriously.” “It sparked a real flurry of kind of planning efforts, of contingency planning efforts, here in Washington,” Lillis said Monday on the network. Meanwhile, the U.S. is continuing to bolster its military presence in the Middle East as Trump weighs his next steps in the conflict. A third American aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the region on Monday, U.S. Central Command said in a social media post. The carrier adds to the already substantial U.S. military buildup near Iran, joining the thousands of troops already deployed aboard the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint in the conflict, with commercial shipping continuing to face attacks and other risks. The waterway, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, has seen traffic fall to less than a third of prewar levels, according to independent maritime assessments cited by the Associated Press. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said mines had damaged six oil tankers since Sunday. The conflict has also contributed to higher costs for Americans, particularly at the gas pump, as disruptions to global oil supplies have pushed up energy prices. Gas prices have since eased, falling below $4 per gallon for the first time since July, AAA reported Friday, but remain nearly a dollar higher than a year ago. The national average stood at $3.81 per gallon on Monday. “These trends may continue, as the International Energy Agency has raised its oil production forecast, putting additional pressure on oil prices as shipments ramp up through the Strait of Hormuz,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a statement Monday. “GasBuddy expects the national average price of gasoline to fall this week to its lowest level since March, dropping below $3.72 per gallon.” Vice President JD Vance defended the administration's handling of the Iran war in an interview with Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday. Vance said Trump could either end the military campaign or apply further military and diplomatic pressure on Iran, but insisted the president would not allow the conflict to become a prolonged commitment. “We are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or, frankly, even a two-year commitment, despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever,” Vance said. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Steven Frank and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: U.S. officials are reportedly assessing intelligence about a potential Iranian plot targeting senior administration officials.

news.text:
Parts of Kyiv were left without electricity and water after Russian forces struck two major bridges across the Dnipro River and other critical infrastructure in a massive overnight missile and drone attack on Ukraine.

news.title: Stocks tumble on Wall Street as Nvidia leads another sell-off in technology companies
news.text: NEW YORK — More drops for stocks in the artificial intelligence industry dragged the US market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.The weakness for tech stocks helped knock the S&P 500 index 1.9% lower and pushed the Nasdaq composite index to a 2.5% loss. The Dow also fell sharply as losses broadened into other sectors. AI-focused companies were by far the biggest weights on the market and have been behind much of the recent turbulence on Wall Street.Nvidia sank 4.1% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership. The company has lost $735 billion in market value since the scandal erupted about CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelities and his ties to an alleged Chinese spy.Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow.Now, following Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities.It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaken by criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers.“The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.”The sector is also now facing more scrutiny from the U.S. government. The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers.Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.9% and notched its second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. Advanced Micro Devices fell 5.6%.CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 6.1%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 4.9%.The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations.Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 3.9% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation.Summit Therapeutics sank 16.5% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer.Tyson Foods rose 8.7% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier.Overall, the S&P 500 shed 145.08 points to close at 7,416.59, marking the third straight loss for the benchmark index. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.4%, to 51,608.17. The Nasdaq composite fell 626.52 points to 24,509.76.The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates.In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation.The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates.Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 3.5% to $92.44. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe.

news.title: OPINION | Trump, Xi, Putin Talks: Why India Must Build Its Own Strategic Power
news.text:
The possibility of a meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen has generated considerable interest in international diplomatic circles. Such a gathering of three influential global powers could have far-reaching implications for the evolving international order. Questions surrounding the Ukraine conflict, economic sanctions, nuclear security, trade disputes and geopolitical competition could feature prominently in their discussions. However, beneath the spectacle of great-power diplomacy lies a fundamental question: can a handful of powerful nations determine the future of the world without adequately considering the interests of others?
The emerging international environment is increasingly described as multipolar. Yet, multipolarity cannot simply mean replacing the dominance of one superpower with an arrangement in which three or four powerful countries divide geopolitical influence among themselves. A genuinely multipolar world must recognise the sovereignty, strategic interests and independent decision-making capacity of nations beyond the traditional centres of power. Otherwise, the proposed international order could become another version of traditional great-power politics.
The proposed Trump-Xi-Putin engagement is significant because all three leaders represent countries with substantial military, economic and diplomatic influence. Washington seeks to maintain its international leadership while addressing economic and security challenges. Beijing wants greater geopolitical influence and protection of its economic interests. Moscow seeks to preserve its strategic position and overcome Western pressure. Their competing priorities could create opportunities for diplomatic negotiations. However, any understanding that disregards the interests of other nations risks creating new geopolitical fault lines.
Lessons From History: Why Great Power Bargains Risk Instability
History offers important lessons. The Yalta Conference of 1945, involving Winston Churchill, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin, demonstrated how decisions taken by victorious powers could shape the political future of entire regions. Although today's circumstances are substantially different, the underlying concern remains relevant: international arrangements negotiated without sufficient consideration of affected nations can generate long-term resentment and instability.
The world of 2026 is not the world of 1945. Economic interdependence is deeper, technological capabilities are more widely distributed, and emerging powers possess greater diplomatic influence. Countries such as India, Japan, Brazil, Indonesia and Australia are consequential actors in global supply chains, energy markets, maritime security and technological development. Any international arrangement that overlooks these realities risks becoming ineffective.
Why India Must Move Beyond Strategic Autonomy
For India, the proposed diplomatic engagement deserves particular attention. New Delhi has consistently advocated strategic autonomy, maintaining relationships with Washington, Moscow and other major powers while preserving independent positions on international issues. Its relationship with Russia remains important for defence cooperation and energy security, while its strategic partnership with the United States has expanded across defence technology, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and the Indo-Pacific. China, meanwhile, remains a significant strategic challenge, particularly because of unresolved border tensions and its expanding regional influence.
India must therefore move from merely articulating strategic autonomy to institutionalising it through concrete policy instruments.
Building Economic And Defence Capabilities
First, New Delhi should establish a comprehensive national economic security framework that integrates foreign policy, defence planning, trade, technology and industrial strategy. A dedicated economic security mechanism under the National Security Council Secretariat could periodically assess vulnerabilities arising from excessive dependence on individual countries for semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, telecommunications equipment, energy resources and defence components. Such assessments should identify alternative suppliers, vulnerable industrial sectors and essential strategic reserves. Economic security must become an integral component of national security rather than remain confined to trade policy.
Second, India must accelerate defence indigenisation. Strategic autonomy is difficult to sustain when essential military platforms, engines, sensors, ammunition, electronic warfare systems and advanced components depend heavily on foreign suppliers. New Delhi should establish time-bound indigenisation targets for critical defence technologies, strengthen collaboration between DRDO, public-sector defence enterprises, private manufacturers and start-ups, and expand investment in indigenous research and development. Joint ventures with foreign partners should prioritise technology transfer, domestic manufacturing, intellectual property development and Indian engineering capabilities rather than permanent dependence on imported systems. Defence exports should also become a central instrument of India's diplomatic influence.
Securing Critical Minerals And Technological Sovereignty
Third, critical-mineral security must receive the same strategic priority as energy security. Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare-earth elements are essential for electric vehicles, renewable energy, semiconductors and advanced defence technologies. India should combine domestic exploration with overseas mineral acquisitions, long-term supply agreements and strategic partnerships across Africa, Latin America and Australia. It must simultaneously invest in domestic refining, processing, recycling and advanced-material manufacturing. Merely importing raw materials from different countries without developing processing capabilities would reproduce existing dependencies in another form.
Fourth, India must pursue technological sovereignty without embracing technological isolation. The government should create stronger incentives for indigenous semiconductor design, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity, telecommunications and advanced manufacturing. Public procurement, research funding and industry-academia partnerships should support commercially viable Indian technologies. International technology partnerships should be negotiated around co-development, intellectual property sharing and the development of domestic engineering expertise. India's objective should be to become an indispensable contributor to global technology ecosystems rather than merely an expanding consumer market.
Strengthening India's Maritime And Regional Security
Fifth, New Delhi should strengthen its maritime and regional security architecture. The Indian Ocean remains central to India's strategic interests, connecting major energy routes, commercial shipping networks and critical maritime infrastructure. India should expand naval modernisation, maritime domain awareness, coastal surveillance and cooperation with friendly countries. The QUAD should be used more effectively for maritime security, resilient supply chains, emerging technologies and disaster response. At the same time, India should strengthen bilateral relationships with Southeast Asian countries and Indian Ocean island nations. Its neighbourhood policy must combine security cooperation with infrastructure development, connectivity, trade and capacity-building.
Seeking Greater Representation In Global Institutions
Sixth, India should demand greater representation in international decision-making institutions. Reform of the United Nations Security Council, greater participation in global financial governance and a stronger voice for developing economies must remain diplomatic priorities. India should also deepen cooperation through BRICS, the G20, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and other multilateral platforms without allowing membership in any grouping to compromise its independent foreign policy. Strategic autonomy must be accompanied by strategic participation.
Finally, India must develop a more proactive diplomatic mechanism for responding to great-power negotiations. Before and after major international summits, New Delhi should engage Washington, Beijing, Moscow, Tokyo, Canberra and European capitals to communicate its red lines and identify areas of cooperation. Any arrangement affecting India's security, territorial integrity, regional stability or economic interests should be assessed independently. India must also maintain consistent diplomatic engagement with its neighbours so that external powers do not exploit regional economic and political vulnerabilities.
Multipolarity Must Respect The Sovereignty Of All Nations
These recommendations are not an argument for confrontation with any major power. They are an argument for building national capabilities that make India less vulnerable to external pressure. Strategic autonomy cannot rest on diplomatic balancing alone; it must be supported by industrial strength, military preparedness, technological innovation and economic resilience.
Ultimately, a stable international order cannot emerge from a division of influence among Washington, Beijing and Moscow. Great powers certainly have responsibilities in managing global crises, but their influence must not become a licence to determine the destinies of others. India should welcome every diplomatic initiative that reduces conflict and promotes international stability while firmly defending the principle that sovereign nations have the right to shape their own futures.
India's objective should not merely be to secure a place at the table where great powers negotiate. It should be to develop sufficient economic, military, technological and diplomatic strength to ensure that no arrangement concerning the future of Asia or the wider world can be sustained without taking India's interests seriously. That is the foundation of meaningful multipolarity.

US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff and US leader’s son-in-law Jared Kushner plan to discuss security guarantees for Kiev and a plan to rebuild the Ukrainian economy with representatives of Europe and Ukraine on November 19, the Axios news portal reported, citing a US administration official.

On November 16, the Chinese Foreign Ministry confirmed that Xi Jinping would hold a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump on November 19. The White House later confirmed these plans as well.

Russia, the United States, and Ukraine held negotiations on November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi to discuss a new system of continental security in the post-conflict period.  US flights nearly back to normal after rare no take-off order 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — United States (US) air travel returned to near-normal on Monday after a rare no-takeoff order left travelLers stranded on airport floors from coast to coast over the weekend.

At least 350 flights into, out of, or within the United States were cancelled Monday, according to tracker FlightAware, far fewer than the 9,200 cancelled when the ground stop order was handed down on Friday.

As he departed for a trip to China earlier Monday, President Donald Trump blamed “old equipment, broken equipment” and the previous administration for a communications failure that saw federal aviation authorities halt takeoffs nationwide for only the second time since the 9/11 attacks.

“We’ve been trying to get the money for two years to fix it,” Trump told reporters, punting the problem to Congress.

The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that old networking equipment in Arkansas — and possibly in Texas — became overloaded, creating a communications failure that cascaded across 17 of the nation’s 22 major air control centres.

It was the longest nationwide halt to takeoffs since 9/11, and the cancellations rippled through the industry, with planes stranded at airports where they were not needed and crews reaching limits on how long they could work.

United Airlines separately reported a widespread outage on Monday that briefly delayed departures before it was resolved.

The Trump administration has been at pains to say during Friday’s ground stop that there was no threat to safety and that the disruption was not the result of a cyberattack.

Instead, it was “an old system that went down, and went down everywhere” after “it got overloaded,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday night, before rebuffing calls for his resignation over the weekend.

Earlier in the week, Duffy had asked Congress for more than $30 billion to upgrade and modernise the US air traffic control system.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said “we implemented a nationwide ground stop out of an abundance of caution” and that “throughout the disruption, certain radio frequencies and radar feeds remained operational, allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft.”

The nationwide halt was lifted at 8:15 pm Friday (0115 GMT Saturday) after about four hours, but untangling the mess of mislocated planes and personnel — and thousands of passengers who needed to be rebooked — continued into Monday.

Duffy upped his appeal to US lawmakers for additional funding late Friday, saying he needed $50 billion to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the government’s purse strings, to provide the money.

“This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding,” Duffy said at the White House. “This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion.”

The last major outage, in January 2023, saw all US departures halted after a different system, the Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) communications network, malfunctioned.

In that case, the FAA blamed software rather than hardware, saying a “damaged database file” was likely the cause. The takeoff halt lasted just under two hours

news.title: Fetterman Would Be Welcomed 'With Open Arms' to Republican Party: Ted Cruz
news.text: Republican U.S. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas says that his party would welcome Democratic Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania with "open arms" should he decide to switch allegiances if Democrats select Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland as their new Senate majority leader. In a post to X on Monday, the Texas lawmaker said, "Sen. John Fetterman is a friend and if he ever decided to become a Republican, we’d welcome him with open arms. More on Verdict where we break down the fact there is a pro-Hamas contingent within the Democrat Party: Nationwide Airstop, Drone Assassination Threat & Dems May Drive Fetterman Out." The post highlighted a lengthier conversation he had alongside conservative commentator Ben Ferguson on the senator's podcast, The Verdict with Ted Cruz. The remarks come as tension within the Democratic Party seemingly grows as Fetterman, one of Israel's staunchest supporters, sees low favorability ratings among Democrats. He also recently said he could reach a breaking point within his own party if Van Hollen, a critic of the Israeli government, gets elected Senate majority leader over Senator Chuck Schumer of New York. The apparent intraparty conflict among Democrats arrives on the heels of sweeping midterm wins for the party. Cruz, now the lone GOP leader in Texas statewide office, said on his podcast earlier this month that the results were not a blue wave; they were a "blue tsunami." He added that the election wins for Democrats were a "Watergate-level repudiation." President Donald Trump conceded partially that the landslide Democratic wins could be due to the war in Iran, although he said he would still do it again. Newsweek reached out to Fetterman's office via email on Monday night for comment. What To Know Cruz continued on his podcast that the Democratic Party is facing a "hostile takeover" of communists and Islamists. He said that it is starting to take shape within the battle for Senate majority leader as the progressive wing of the party has broken with Schumer. Cruz pointed to the "very liberal" Van Hollen challenging Schumer as an example, while adding that he believes Schumer will ultimately win the race for majority leader. He did predict that Schumer will not run for office again in New York, and this will be his last two years in his Senate seat. "John Fetterman has shown incredible courage standing up to the crazies in his party," Cruz said. He later called the Democratic Party brazenly anti-Israel, saying there is a real "pro-Hamas contingent." Newsweek reached out to the Democratic National Committee for comment. "Fetterman, I'll tell ya, if he became a Republican, we would welcome him enthusiastically. John is a friend, I like him. I will say the Republican senators treat Fetterman much better than the Democrats do. The Democrats hate his guts, and they're really vicious to him," Cruz said. The potential of Fetterman jumping ship comes with a few caveats, a political analyst pointed out. Grant Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek on Monday, "It would be good for Republicans, to have one more addition to their caucus in the Senate, and to lessen the Democrats’ majority by one. But a lot of Fetterman’s positions and views do not fit well with the Republican Party, and he has stated many times that he does not see himself as a Republican and is not interested in changing parties. More likely he would do something similar to Joe Lieberman and become an independent." Reeher continued, "It’s hard to imagine Fetterman surviving a primary challenge in his next re-election, assuming he pursues one. I imagine he will retire instead. It’s a certainty that he will face a primary challenge from a high-quality candidate to his Left, and that candidate will no doubt be backed by some high-profile Democrats, like AOC, El Sayed, etc. The party has shifted to the Left and a senator like Fetterman is no longer welcome." What Fetterman Said About Van Hollen While speaking with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany over the weekend, Fetterman was asked if there was a red line for him regarding potentially switching parties. "Yeah, absolutely, it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen, that has really made his name being very...hostile to Israel." Fetterman questioned why not be angry or hostile toward Iran, Hamas or Hezbollah in the region. "Their first instincts are to punish Israel and to withhold these kinds of aid. Why isn't your first instinct to say let's hold Iran accountable?" Fetterman said while acknowledging the recent spike in gas prices impacting American households. The senator said, when asked again if he'd switch parties, that he is a Democrat. "I don't expect my party to change, but I'm always going to put our country before party and I'm going to look for and extend my hand for bipartisanship," he told McEnany. What Polls and Prediction Markets Show An August survey by The New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena Research Institute, shows that Fetterman's net favorability among Pennsylvania registered voters was 46 percent compared to a 41 percent unfavorable rating. Among those identifying as Democrats, Fetterman's favorability rating was 22 percent, versus a 63 percent unfavorable rating. Among Republican identifiers, Fetterman's favorability was 73 percent compared to a 21 percent unfavorable rating. The poll surveyed 760 voters in Pennsylvania from August 17 to August 21 and had a margin of error of 4.5 percent among registered voters. Prediction market site Kalshi shows 32 percent that Fetterman will leave the Democratic Party before August 2027, around 10 p.m. Monday. The prediction market also shows 29 percent that he will leave before January 1, 2028, and 25 percent before April 1, 2027. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins

news.title: Xi and Carney call for deeper ties as Canada looks beyond US for trade
news.text:
The leaders of China and Canada called for deeper ties Tuesday as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.

The meeting came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry.

“Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.”

Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship.

“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” he said.

Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
news.summary: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing

news.title: Archival urges unity after protesters, police clash at rally
news.text: CEBU CITY — Cebu City Mayor Nestor Archival has urged residents to set aside anger and divisiveness following the confrontation between police and protesters during Monday's anti-Pax Silica rally along Colon Street, amid reports of injured demonstrators and journalists.In a statement on Tuesday, Nov. 17, Archival expressed regret over the confrontation, recognizing both the protesters who exercised their right to express their views and the police personnel responsible for maintaining peace and order.He said the reported burning of an effigy raised public safety concerns that required police attention, but also said that law enforcers must exercise restraint, professionalism and respect for human rights in carrying out their duties.“The tension and emotions during the incident may have contributed to the escalation,” Archival said.He apologized to those affected and urged the public to treat the incident as a lesson rather than allow it to create further discord.The mayor added that freedom of expression and public safety must both be upheld as essential elements of a peaceful and democratic society.He also reiterated that protecting the safety, welfare and rights of every Cebuano remains his priority.“Magtinahuray ug magtinabangay ta (Let us respect and help each other). Let us choose dialogue over confrontation, understanding over anger, and unity over division,” Archival said.Meanwhile, the University of the Philippines Cebu College of Communication, Art and Design (CCAD) condemned the dispersal of protesters and the reported use of excessive force against individuals exercising their constitutional rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.In a statement on Tuesday, CCAD cited Section 4, Article III of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, which guarantees freedom of speech, expression and the press, as well as the right of people to peaceably assemble and petition the government for redress of grievances.The college said these rights must be respected regardless of the causes, positions or grievances expressed during public demonstrations.It reminded law enforcement authorities to observe maximum tolerance under Section 3(c) of Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, which requires the highest degree of restraint during public assemblies and their dispersal.CCAD also recognized demonstrations as important spaces for citizens, particularly the youth and marginalized sectors, to raise concerns, question institutions and demand accountability.“Peaceful dissent is not a threat to democracy; it is an essential expression of it,” the college said.It warned that maintaining public order should not justify suppressing legitimate grievances, intimidating protesters or silencing demands for accountability.The college further emphasized the importance of protecting journalists and media workers covering demonstrations, saying their safety is essential to the public's right to information and the media's role in holding institutions accountable.It called for an impartial investigation into the dispersal, accountability for any abuses committed and protection of the rights and safety of all protesters.The confrontation on Nov. 16 also drew criticism from media and human rights organizations following reports of injuries among protesters and two journalists.The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines Cebu reported that one journalist was struck by a police shield, while another inhaled fire extinguisher powder discharged by police personnel.NUJP Cebu urged the Cebu City Police Office (CCPO) and Police Regional Office Central Visayas to investigate the incident and hold accountable officers found responsible. It also called for the protection of student journalists who covered the demonstration.The University of the Philippines Cebu Committee for the Promotion and Protection of Academic Freedom and Human Rights also called for an impartial investigation and accountability, reminding police to observe maximum tolerance.Human rights group Karapatan Central Visayas alleged that police officers wearing riot gear manhandled protesters, discharged fire extinguishers directly at them and attempted to arrest 15 demonstrators.Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas Cebu separately reported injuries among protesters and around five attempted arrests, including those involving peasant advocates.The CCPO, however, maintained that its personnel did not initiate violence and acted to maintain public order and protect public safety.In a statement Monday night, the police office said it was open to an impartial investigation into the reported injuries of the two journalists. news.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite backing from big names
news.text:
Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, three people have told Reuters.

Mr Huang was forced to step down last week amid revelations about affairs involving employees and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The former chief executive's departure plunged the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sent shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.

More than 180,200 people, including thousands identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, have signed a petition demanding Mr Huang's return.

Elon Musk has also thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump, who reportedly held millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, said he would not mind seeing Mr Huang reinstated as CEO.

Mr Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $US13 million ($19m) and $US62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.

Campaign gaining traction

Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen".

It came as the Stand With Jensen campaign gained traction online.

"We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter published on the campaign's website said.

The campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories.

Prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace Mr Huang before all the facts are known.

However, a person familiar with the matter said: "The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back."

Large investors are risk-averse

The uncertainty over Mr Huang's future has divided investors and complicated the board's search for a successor.

Nvidia has lost $US800 billion in market value since Mr Huang stepped down.

The company's shares closed down more than 4 per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker was due to report third-quarter earnings.

Independent technology researcher Richard Windsor said he expected "very risk-averse" large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Mr Huang's return while investigations remained unresolved, because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create.

At the centre of the scandal is Chinese businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang (no relation), who Mr Huang admitted to having an affair with.

US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, sources said.

Huang's exit rocks Taiwan

Mr Huang's reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed "Jensanity".

Nvidia relies on a local manufacturer to make its most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture other chips and systems underpinning the AI boom.

For many Taiwanese, Mr Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global AI boom.

Jimmy Yang, a 42-year-old marketing worker, said Mr Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan.

He expressed hope that Mr Huang could eventually return to Nvidia.

"His private life is his own choice," Mr Yang said. 

"But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive," he said.

Reuters/ABC
news.summary: Nvidia is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, despite a growing campaign for his return.
news.author: ABC News

news.title: No hacks of US aviation regulator detected by intelligence — transportation secretary
news.text:
NEW YORK, November 17. /TASS/. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) system was not hacked on Friday, when a massive disruption to air traffic occurred across the country, all US intelligence agencies have concluded, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated.

"We had all of our intelligence agencies at Donald Trump’s direction talk on Friday night. No one was seeing any kind of hack into our system," he said in an interview with Fox News. "So I think it was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error."

On November 13, the US Federal Aviation Administration suspended all departures nationwide for more than four hours due to a communications outage at air traffic control centers. This was the longest nationwide flight suspension in 25 years: more than 10,000 flights were canceled on Friday and Saturday. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the disruption to what has been described as an incredibly old air traffic control system whose routers were unable to handle the overload.
news.summary: It was a network problem or a router problem or an installation error, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said
news.author: Tass

news.title: US intel indicates Iran is drawing up plans for potential ‘dirty bomb’ attack in Washington: Report
news.text: WASHINGTON: Fresh American intelligence indicates that Iran is formulating strategies to target high-ranking Trump administration figures in Washington, DC, using a "dirty bomb" or chemical weapon, CNN has reported, citing multiple US officials.The sources cited in the report noted that the intelligence showed no signs of an imminent attack, with Iranian actors instead mapping out plans to secure alternative options should they choose to move forward. Nonetheless, the plotting is reportedly highly detailed, identifying specific locations and targets, thereby triggering US contingency preparations."Whether they actually have the personnel in place to execute is a matter of debate," one of the sources told CNN.According to information provided to the cable network by a source, US intelligence has intercepted Iranian claims concerning bomb-making materials allegedly concealed inside the United States. CNN reported that while authorities remain divided over the validity of the intelligence, they largely agree that it would be entirely straightforward and plausible for Tehran to have stashed nuclear or chemical substances within the US that could be packaged alongside conventional explosives to form a so-called dirty bomb."Any weapon like that is a weapon of terror, not a weapon of precision, just like a suicide bomber blowing themselves up," one of the sources said. "They can make people really sick and certain areas uninhabitable.".Iran committed to diplomacy, US chose ‘different path’, says Araghchi.Amid these rising regional tensions, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani on Monday (local time).
